title: SQL Subqueries, CTEs and Set Operators
summary: Quick revision notes on scalar, IN, EXISTS and correlated subqueries, derived tables, CTEs, recursive CTEs, and UNION vs UNION ALL, from mental model to a final cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Subqueries and CTEs: The Mental Model
points: A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement; the inner result is treated as a value, a list, or a table depending on where it sits
Scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column, usable wherever an expression fits: SELECT name, (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp) AS top FROM emp
Derived table is a subquery in FROM and needs an alias in most engines (PostgreSQL 16+ and SQLite do not require one): FROM (SELECT dept, AVG(salary) a FROM emp GROUP BY dept) d
CTE is a named result set defined with WITH name AS (...) and valid only for the one statement that follows it
Placement decides the shape: WHERE/SELECT take a scalar or list, FROM takes a table, and a CTE can be referenced like a table several times

chapters.title: IN, EXISTS and Correlated Subqueries
points: IN compares a value against a list the subquery returns: WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT id FROM dept WHERE city='Pune')
EXISTS returns true if the subquery yields at least one row and ignores the selected columns, so SELECT 1 is conventional
Correlated subquery references a column of the outer query and is logically re-evaluated per outer row: WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e1.dept_id)
EXISTS stops at the first match and is NULL-safe, while IN builds or probes a list and is easier to read for small static lists
Anti-join: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.cust_id = c.id) finds customers with no orders

chapters.title: CTEs and Recursive CTEs
points: Basic CTE syntax: WITH high AS (SELECT * FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000) SELECT * FROM high; chain several with commas: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...)
Use a CTE over a nested derived table to name each step and reference it more than once; it does not guarantee materialization, which depends on the engine
Recursive CTE has an anchor member, UNION ALL, then a recursive member that references the CTE itself, and it stops when the recursive step returns no rows
Org-chart example: WITH RECURSIVE t AS (SELECT id, boss_id, 1 AS lvl FROM emp WHERE boss_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.boss_id, t.lvl+1 FROM emp e JOIN t ON e.boss_id = t.id) SELECT * FROM t
Cyclic data loops forever, so add a depth cap such as WHERE t.lvl < 10 or use the engine's cycle limit; SQL Server omits the RECURSIVE keyword and defaults to a 100-level limit

chapters.title: UNION vs UNION ALL and Choosing a Form
points: UNION appends result sets and removes duplicate rows, which needs a sort or hash step
UNION ALL appends and keeps every row, is faster, and is the right default when duplicates are impossible or wanted
Both inputs need the same column count, compatible types by position, and column names come from the first SELECT
ORDER BY applies once to the whole combined result and goes at the very end
Choosing: single value means scalar subquery, membership test means IN, existence test means EXISTS, reused or readable steps mean CTE, hierarchy means recursive CTE

chapters.title: Common Mistakes with Subqueries and Set Operators
points: NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery list contains a NULL, because x <> NULL is unknown, so use NOT EXISTS or filter NULLs out
A scalar subquery returning more than one row raises an error; guard it with a unique key, MAX(), or LIMIT 1
Forgetting the alias on a derived table fails in most engines, as in FROM (SELECT ...) d
Using UNION when UNION ALL is enough adds a needless sort and silently drops legitimate duplicate rows

Recursive CTE without a termination condition loops forever on cyclic data under UNION ALL; UNION discards rows already produced and can stop a simple cycle, but not once a changing column such as a depth counter makes every row distinct

chapters.title: Subqueries, CTEs and Set Operators Cheat Sheet
points: Scalar: (SELECT MAX(x) FROM t) returns one row and one column, usable in SELECT, WHERE or HAVING
List and existence: col IN (SELECT ...) versus EXISTS (SELECT 1 ... WHERE inner.k = outer.k); prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN
Table forms: derived table FROM (SELECT ...) alias; CTE WITH name AS (SELECT ...) SELECT ... FROM name
Recursive skeleton: WITH RECURSIVE r AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive-step) SELECT * FROM r, with a depth cap
Set operators: UNION dedupes, UNION ALL keeps all and is faster; matching column count and types, one final ORDER BY
